section.title: Paul's Rights as an Apostle
section.sectionRationale: Having told the strong to lay down their freedom for the sake of a weaker brother, Paul now offers himself as the living proof. He is a free man and a genuine apostle with every right to material support and to a believing wife, yet he refuses to use those rights so that nothing will hinder the gospel. The chapter turns the abstract argument of chapter eight into a portrait: a man who gladly surrenders what is his to win others to Christ, and who disciplines himself like an athlete so that after preaching to others he will not be disqualified.
section.thesis: A true apostle with real rights lays them down for the gospel, becoming a slave to all and all things to all people so that by all possible means he might save some, and he runs and trains with strict discipline for an imperishable crown, lest after preaching to others he himself be disqualified.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Paul the free apostle and his rights; the many witnesses that gospel workers deserve support; the rights he surrenders because he is compelled to preach; and the great turn, becoming all things to all people and running to win the imperishable crown.

verses.text: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you yourselves not my workmanship in the Lord?
Even if I am not an apostle to others, surely I am to you. For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.
This is my defense to those who scrutinize me:
Have we no right to food and to drink?
Have we no right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the Lord’s brothers and Cephas?
Or are Barnabas and I the only apostles who must work for a living?
Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not drink of its milk?
Do I say this from a human perspective? Doesn’t the Law say the same thing?
For it is written in the Law of Moses: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.” Is it about oxen that God is concerned?
Isn’t He actually speaking on our behalf? Indeed, this was written for us, because when the plowman plows and the thresher threshes, they should also expect to share in the harvest.
If we have sown spiritual seed among you, is it too much for us to reap a material harvest from you?
If others have this {{exousia|right}} to your support, shouldn’t we have it all the more? But we did not exercise this right. Instead, we put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ.
Do you not know that those who work in the temple eat of its food, and those who serve at the altar partake of its offerings?
In the same way, the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the {{euangelion|gospel}}.
But I have not used any of these rights. And I am not writing this to suggest that something be done for me. Indeed, I would rather die than let anyone nullify my boast.
Yet when I preach the gospel, I have no reason to boast, because I am obligated to preach. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!
If my preaching is voluntary, I have a reward. But if it is not voluntary, I am still entrusted with a responsibility.
What then is my reward? That in preaching the gospel I may offer it free of charge, and so not use up my rights in preaching it.

units.label: All things to all, run to win

verses.text: Though I am free of obligation to anyone, I make myself {{douloo|a slave}} to everyone, to win as many as possible.
To the Jews I became like a Jew, to win the Jews. To those under the law I became like one under the law (though I myself am not under the law), to win those under the law.
To those without the law I became like one without the law (though I am not outside the law of God but am under the law of Christ), to win those without the law.
To the weak I became weak, to win the weak. I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some.
I do all this for the sake of the gospel, so that I may share in its blessings.
Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? Run in such a way as to take the prize.
Everyone who competes in the games trains with strict discipline. They do it for a crown that is perishable, but we do it for a {{stephanos|crown}} that is imperishable.
Therefore I do not run aimlessly; I do not fight like I am beating the air.
No, I discipline my body and make it my slave, so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be {{adokimos|disqualified}}.

exousia.gloss: Right, authority, freedom to act. Paul insists he holds a real exousia to material support, the same right he grants to others, yet he chooses not to use it. The word matters to the whole argument: freedom is genuine only if you are truly free to lay it down for love's sake.

euangelion.gloss: Gospel, good news, the announcement of what God has done in Christ crucified and risen. It is the hinge of the chapter: the Lord Himself has arranged that gospel workers live from the gospel, yet the same gospel is so precious to Paul that he waives his living rather than put any obstacle in its way.

douloo.gloss: To enslave, to make a slave. Though free from all, Paul enslaves himself to everyone to win as many as possible. It is a deliberate echo of Christ, who took the form of a servant; freedom in Christ expresses itself not in self-assertion but in glad self-lowering for the good of others.

stephanos.gloss: A victor's wreath or crown, the garland awarded to the winner of the games. The athlete disciplines himself for a wreath that withers; the believer runs for a crown that never fades. It names the imperishable reward of those who finish faithfully in Christ.

adokimos.gloss: Failing the test, rejected, disqualified. Paul fears that a preacher who does not discipline himself could, like an athlete breaking the rules, be ruled out. It is a sober warning that gifting and preaching are no substitute for a life of persevering, self-controlled faith.

basic.context: Paul has just told the Corinthians who have knowledge to give up their freedom to eat idol food for the sake of a weaker brother. Now he shows them how it is done, using his own life. He really is a free man and a real apostle, with every right to be paid for his work and to travel with a wife, as Peter and the other apostles did. Yet he refused to take a penny from the Corinthians, working with his own hands instead, so that no one could ever accuse him of preaching for money and so hinder the gospel. He made himself a servant of everyone, adapting to Jew and Gentile, weak and strong, to win as many as possible. And he compares the Christian life to an athlete in training, running to win a crown that will never fade.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter is a worked example, not a change of subject. Paul is defending his apostleship, but chiefly he is modelling the very love he asked for in chapter eight: rights freely surrendered so that others may be saved. The right to support is real and Christ commanded it, yet love can lay a real right down. Read verse 27 rightly: it is a call to persevere and discipline oneself, not a claim that a believer can lose salvation by a single slip.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul holds a real exousia, a right, to material support, yet will not use it. He waives his living for the sake of the euangelion, the gospel, which he must preach. Though free from all, he uses the strong word douloo, to enslave himself, to everyone to win them. And he runs like an athlete for a stephanos, a victor's crown, that is imperishable, disciplining himself lest he be adokimos, disqualified.
basic.typology: The temple and the altar point forward: as the priests of Israel lived from the offerings, so gospel ministers live from the gospel, the shadow fulfilled in the new covenant ministry. The athlete's crown, a fading wreath in the games, foreshadows the imperishable crown Christ gives to those who finish the race by faith.
basic.christ: Behind Paul's self-surrender stands Christ Himself, who though rich became poor, who took the form of a servant and made Himself nothing to win us. When Paul enslaves himself to all to save some, he is imitating his Lord. The gospel he refuses to hinder is the message of Christ crucified, and the imperishable crown he runs for is given by Christ, the righteous Judge.
basic.god: God is the one who prescribed that those who preach the gospel should live from it, and God is the one who compels Paul with a holy necessity, woe to me if I do not preach. He rewards faithful labour and He is the searcher who will test each servant's work. He calls His people to a disciplined, persevering life, and He supplies the grace to run.
basic.crossReferences: In the Gospels Jesus says the worker is worthy of his wages. Philippians tells of the Son who emptied Himself and took the form of a servant. Second Timothy speaks of finishing the race and the crown of righteousness. Second Corinthians shows Paul refusing support so as not to burden the churches.
basic.oneStory: The whole Bible moves toward a Saviour who lays down His rights to win a people, and toward a people who, filled with His Spirit, do the same. Paul's surrendered rights and disciplined running are a small picture of the gospel itself: freedom used not for self but for the salvation of others, until the race is finished and the imperishable crown is given.

context.literary:
Chapter 9 looks like a digression, since it breaks off from idol food to talk about Paul himself, but it is the middle panel of a planned three part argument. Chapter 8 states the principle, that love may restrain a right. Chapter 9 shows the principle in a living person. Chapter 10 returns to the Corinthians with a warning and with practical rulings. The chapter is a defence, an apologia, as verse 3 says, though Paul defends himself so as to teach.

The movement is clear. Verses 1 to 6 are a run of rapid questions, most of them expecting the answer yes. Verses 7 to 14 build the case for the right of support from five directions: soldier, farmer, shepherd, the law of Moses, and the practice of the temple, ending with the Lord's own command. Then comes the turn in verses 15 to 18. After proving the right at length, Paul declares that he has used none of it. The proof was never a bid for money. Verses 19 to 23 are the principle of becoming all things to all, built on a repeated phrase, 'to win', which occurs five times. Verses 24 to 27 end with an image from the games.

The chapter also has an inclusio of sorts, since it opens by asking 'Am I not free?' and ends with a man who makes his body a slave. Freedom, in Paul's hands, ends in discipline. And the closing fear of being 'disqualified' prepares for chapter 10, which opens with Israel's example of people who had every privilege and still fell.
context.historical:
Corinth was a city of wandering teachers. Public speakers who charged fees, and who gathered pupils round them, were a familiar sight, and a teacher who took money from a wealthy patron entered a relationship of obligation. Some at Corinth seem to have thought Paul inferior because he refused to be paid, and they may have taken his work with his hands as a sign of low status, or as proof that he lacked the confidence of a true apostle. Paul's refusal was therefore costly and misunderstood, which is why he feels the need to defend it here and again in 2 Corinthians 11:7-9.

Paul made his living as a tentmaker, Acts 18:3. He worked beside Priscilla and Aquila, and in other letters he reminds churches that he worked night and day so as not to burden anyone, 1 Thessalonians 2:9. In the ancient world manual work was thought beneath a free man of standing, so the apostle's workshop was a deliberate choice of humility.

The examples Paul draws on were everyday ones. A soldier was supplied by the army, a vineyard owner ate his grapes, a shepherd drank the milk, and an ox treading grain on the threshing floor ate as it went. The temple practice he cites was equally familiar, since priests in Israel lived from the offerings, Numbers 18:8-24. The closing image would have been vivid to a Corinthian, because the Isthmian Games were held near the city every two years, and the athletes who competed trained for months for a wreath that would wither within days.
context.canonical:
The proof text in verse 9 is Deuteronomy 25:4, 'Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.' Paul reads a law about animals as having a point for the people who serve, and he says it was written 'for us.' Paul uses the same verse in 1 Timothy 5:17-18, where he pairs it with a saying of Jesus, 'The worker is worthy of his wages,' which also stands in Luke 10:7. The 'Lord has prescribed' of verse 14 therefore points to the instruction Jesus gave when He sent out the Twelve and the seventy-two, Matthew 10:10 and Luke 10:7.

The priests who live from the altar come from the Law, Numbers 18:8-24 and Deuteronomy 18:1-5. Paul sees a continuing principle there: those who serve in sacred things are supported by those they serve.

Paul's refusal to use the right appears again in 2 Corinthians 11:7-9 and in the speech at Miletus, where he tells the Ephesian elders that his own hands supplied his needs, Acts 20:33-35. His account of becoming 'all things to all people' is echoed by Acts 16:3, where he circumcises Timothy, and held in tension with Galatians 2:3-5, where he refuses to circumcise Titus. The athletic images return in Philippians 3:12-14, 2 Timothy 4:7-8 and Hebrews 12:1-2. And the 'law of Christ,' which Paul says he is under in verse 21, appears again in Galatians 6:2, where it is fulfilled by bearing one another's burdens.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul meant the Corinthians to see that what he was asking of them in chapter 8 was nothing he had not already done. He was not a man who had never held any rights and so found it easy to speak of giving them up. He had the full right of an apostle: to be fed, to travel with a wife, to be paid. He proved it by argument, by the law, and by the Lord's command. Then he laid it down. His credentials in the argument are what give weight to his example.

He also meant to defend his apostleship against those who sneered at it. The Corinthians themselves, he says, are the seal of it, verse 2. A church that had been founded by his preaching could hardly question the one who founded it. And he meant them to understand why he refused their money. It was not because money is evil or because he thought ministers should not be supported. It was to keep the gospel free of any suspicion of being sold, and to offer it 'free of charge,' verse 18.

Finally, the closing section is meant to stir them from complacency. Paul presents the Christian life as a discipline that costs effort, with a prize at the end, and he uses himself as an example of someone who takes the possibility of failure seriously.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a single apostle's choices, and it should not be turned into a universal rule in either direction. Paul does not command that every pastor refuse a salary. He affirms in verse 14, on the authority of the Lord, that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from it, and in Galatians 6:6 he tells those who are taught to share with their teachers. His refusal was a free decision for a particular setting, in which the gospel might otherwise have been mistaken for a business.

Nor is the account of 'all things to all people' a licence to change convictions to suit a crowd. Paul says plainly that he was never outside the law of God but under the law of Christ, verse 21. What he adjusts is his manner, his customs and his freedoms. The message and the morals stay fixed.

What does carry forward is the principle that rights are real, and that love may set them aside for the sake of the gospel. It is also a prescription, at the close, for training. Athletes train for a perishable wreath, and believers can give no less to an imperishable one. Paul's own example is a picture of a disciplined life, not a recipe for how to earn salvation.

debates.question: What does Paul fear in being 'disqualified' in verse 27?

views.label: Losing his place in ministry or his reward
views.case: The image is of an athlete ruled out of the contest, not of one who never entered. Paul has 'preached to others', so the loss feared is that of an approved servant, his reward and usefulness. 1 Corinthians 3:12-15 speaks of a work that is burned while its builder is saved, 'but only as through fire,' and that parallels the idea of a loss that falls short of loss of salvation.

views.label: Losing salvation itself
views.case: Others hold that Paul really does allow that a person who preaches the gospel could be rejected at the last. They point to the neighbouring warning of chapter 10 about Israel's fall and to the word adokimos, which Paul uses elsewhere of those who fail the test, 2 Corinthians 13:5-7.

views.label: Proof that a profession is genuine
views.case: A third reading is that Paul treats discipline as the evidence of true faith. A person who has no care for obedience shows that the faith never took root, and Paul's self control is the mark of the real thing. Perseverance is the fruit of grace, not the price of it.

debates.bearing: All three readings agree that Paul takes the danger seriously and refuses to coast. They differ on what the prize and the loss are, and the surrounding chapters, especially chapter 10, press for sober self examination rather than complacency.

debates.question: Is Paul's flexibility in verses 19 to 23 consistent, or does it look like trimming?

views.label: Principled flexibility
views.case: Paul distinguishes between what the gospel demands and what is merely custom. He will keep Jewish customs among Jews and eat Gentile food among Gentiles, but he refuses to make either a condition of salvation. Galatians 2:3-5 shows him standing firm when the truth of the gospel is at stake, and Acts 16:3 shows him bending where nothing is at stake.

views.label: An uneasy compromise
views.case: Critics, ancient and modern, have thought it looks like having it both ways. Paul himself saw the risk, which is why he adds that he is under the law of Christ and that he does all of it for the gospel, never for his own advantage.

debates.bearing: The test Paul gives is the aim, 'to win', and the limit he gives is the law of Christ. Flexibility of method is allowed, and flexibility of truth is not.

study.originalLanguages:
The most important word in the chapter is exousia, 'right' or 'authority,' which Paul uses in verses 4, 5, 6, 12 and 18. In 8:9 the same word was translated 'freedom,' and it is the thread that ties the two chapters together. An exousia is a real authority, not a loophole, and Paul's point is that a real authority can be laid down on purpose.

In verse 3 Paul says 'my defense' and 'those who scrutinize me.' The first is apologia, a formal answer to a charge, and the second is the verb anakrino, to examine as a judge would. Paul used the same verb of the Corinthians' verdict on himself in 4:3. They are putting him on trial, and he answers as a witness. He also calls the church 'the seal' of his apostleship, from sphragis, the stamp that authenticates a document.

Verse 12 says the apostles would put up with anything rather than 'hinder' the gospel. The noun behind it is egkope, a cutting in, the word for an obstacle placed in a road. Paul fears that taking money might become a barrier in the path of the gospel. In verse 15 and verse 18 he speaks of 'using' a right with the verb chraomai, and in verse 18 he adds a prefix, katachraomai, which means to use fully or to use up. He has not used his rights, and he is determined not to use them up.

Verse 16 says he is 'obligated.' The Greek is anagke, necessity, and Paul writes that necessity lies upon him. In verse 17 the 'responsibility' entrusted to him is an oikonomia, a stewardship, the post of a household manager who has been given charge of another man's goods. He is not the owner of the message but its steward.

In verses 19 to 22 the verb kerdaino, to win or gain, is repeated like a drumbeat. The companion verb is douloo, to enslave, in verse 19. A free man makes himself a slave in order to win. In verse 21 Paul calls himself ennomos Christou, 'in the law of Christ,' and his lawfulness is now measured by Christ and not by Moses.

The athletic words are chosen with care. In verse 24 'prize' is brabeion, the award given by the judge, and the runners are told to run 'so as to take it.' In verse 25 the athlete exercises enkrateia, self mastery. In verse 26 Paul says he does not 'fight like beating the air,' a boxing image, and in verse 27 the verb translated 'discipline' is hypopiazo, literally to strike under the eye, to bruise. He treats his own body as an opponent that must be brought into line. The word 'disqualified,' adokimos, is the opposite of dokimos, approved, tested and found genuine.

typology.type: The priests who live from the altar, 1 Corinthians 9:13
typology.fulfillment: The priests of Israel had no land of their own and lived from the offerings, Numbers 18:8-24. Paul says the Lord has set the same principle for the preachers of the gospel. The correspondence is of function: both groups are set apart for sacred service and supported by the people. The escalation is that the altar is now the cross, and the priesthood of the whole church, 1 Peter 2:9, includes those who serve it by proclamation. The type falls short because the old priests were supported by a ritual system, and the new ministers serve a finished sacrifice and must never present themselves as mediators between God and people.

typology.type: The ox on the threshing floor, Deuteronomy 25:4
typology.fulfillment: Paul reads a law about animals as a lesson about workers, and says God has us in view, verse 10. The ox treads out grain and is allowed to eat while it does. This is a pattern of the principle that those who labour should share in the fruit. The correspondence is real, though Paul's reading goes beyond the original setting. In Christ the principle is fulfilled in the Lord's own command, 'The worker is worthy of his wages,' Luke 10:7. It falls short as a type because it shows only the principle of fair reward, and not the deeper truth that the gospel itself is a gift that cannot be bought.

typology.type: The race and the crown, 1 Corinthians 9:24-25
typology.fulfillment: The athletes at the Isthmian Games trained hard for a wreath that would soon wither, and Paul sets that picture beside a crown that lasts. The correspondence is effort for a prize, and the escalation is the nature of the prize. In Christ the believer runs 'looking to Jesus,' Hebrews 12:1-2, and the crown is the 'crown of righteousness' that the righteous Judge will give, 2 Timothy 4:8. It is a picture and falls short in one respect, because the athletic contest has a single winner, while in Christ every faithful runner receives the crown.

study.christ:
Paul does not mention Jesus by name very often in chapter 9, but the whole chapter is shaped by Him. It leads to Christ first by commission. Paul bases his apostleship on having 'seen Jesus our Lord,' verse 1, which points to the meeting on the Damascus road, and he rests the right to support on a command of Jesus, verse 14. The authority behind everything in this passage is the risen Lord who sent him.

It leads to Christ by pattern. The surrender of rights in verses 15 to 19 is a small copy of the deepest surrender in history. The Son who was rich became poor, 2 Corinthians 8:9, and the one who had every right to be treated as God emptied Himself and took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:6-7. When Paul says he made himself a slave to all, he is walking the road his Master walked. Jesus Himself said that He came to serve and to give His life, Mark 10:45, and washed His disciples' feet, John 13:14-15. Paul's argument for giving up rights is Jesus' whole life told in miniature.

It leads to Christ by law. Verse 21 contains a remarkable phrase, that Paul is 'under the law of Christ.' Paul has left Moses as the measure of life, yet he is not lawless. A new standard has come, the pattern of Christ's own love, which Galatians 6:2 says is fulfilled by carrying one another's burdens. The law of Christ is not a second legal code, but the shape that life takes when a person follows the one who loved to the end.

It leads to Christ by reward. The crown is imperishable, and elsewhere Paul says the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award it, 2 Timothy 4:8. The judge at the end of the race is the same Christ who ran before. Hebrews 12:2 calls Him the author and perfecter of our faith, who endured the cross for the joy set before Him. The believer runs as one who follows a leader who has already finished.

A caution is in order. The chapter does not make Paul a second Christ or his sacrifices a part of redemption. What he does is imitate, and the imitation is the effect of the gospel, not its cause. The gospel he will not hinder is the news of what Christ has done, and he spends himself to make it known.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows is that God cares about how His servants are provided for. The Lord 'has prescribed' that preachers live from the gospel, verse 14, and Paul sets the law of Deuteronomy 25:4 beside it, asking whether God's concern in that law was really for oxen, verse 9. The question has an answer: God is concerned with workers, and with justice among those who labour. A God who legislates for the animal on the threshing floor has not forgotten the minister.

Second, God lays a holy necessity on His servants. 'Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!' is not the voice of a man who chose a career. It is the voice of someone under orders, who has been entrusted with a stewardship, verse 17. God's call can be neither bought nor declined, and it makes ordinary calculations of reward look small. Yet He also treats the willing worker as one who earns a reward, verse 17, and so He is both the sovereign who commands and the generous master who pays.

Third, God is the judge who tests. Verse 27 speaks of being found unfit, and Paul's fear is real because the Lord's judgment is real. This is not the fear of a slave before a cruel master, but of a servant before an exacting and good one, who will examine each person's work, 1 Corinthians 3:13. The God who is the righteous Judge is also the God who gives the crown, 2 Timothy 4:8.

Fourth, God is the one who makes a freedom for others. Paul is free of everyone and so can bind himself to everyone, because he is bound first to God. Free service is possible only for those who have a master above all masters. The same God who gives rights also gives the grace to waive them, and neither the right nor its surrender is the product of human strength.

For worship, this means that ministry and discipline are acts of worship before an audience of One. It also means that those who serve are to be honoured and fed, and that those who are served should give gladly. A congregation that starves its teacher and a teacher who exploits the congregation both fail to reflect the God of this chapter.

crossReferences.note: The law about the threshing ox that Paul quotes in verse 9. In its setting it was a rule of kindness to an animal at work. Paul says its deeper point is for the workers who serve, and he uses the same verse again in 1 Timothy 5:18, which shows how much weight he gave to it.

Jesus tells the seventy-two to eat what they are given because the worker is worthy of his wages. This is the saying behind Paul's 'the Lord has prescribed' in verse 14, and it shows that the right to support was not Paul's own invention but a command of Christ.
The priests and Levites received portions from the offerings and the tithes. This is the background of verse 13, and it shows that sacred work has always been supported by those who benefit from it.

Paul tells the Corinthians that he preached to them free of charge, and that other churches supported him while he served them. The passage shows what lay behind his refusal and how much his critics made of it.

The account of Paul's first stay in Corinth, where he joined Aquila and Priscilla and worked with them as a tentmaker while he reasoned in the synagogue. It supplies the practical background to the claim in verse 6 that he and Barnabas worked for a living.

The hymn of the Son who became a servant. This is the pattern behind Paul's decision to make himself a slave to everyone, and it explains why he treats the giving up of rights as the shape of the gospel life.
Carry one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ. It explains the phrase 'under the law of Christ' in verse 21: the law that governs Paul is the way of self giving love.

Paul circumcises Timothy because of the Jews in that area, who knew his father was Greek. It is an example of becoming like a Jew to win Jews, and it contrasts with Galatians 2:3, where he will not compel Titus.

At the end of his life Paul says he has fought the good fight and finished the race, and that the crown of righteousness is laid up for him. It shows that the aim of 1 Corinthians 9:24-27 was reached, and that the crown is given by the Lord.
The call to run with endurance, looking to Jesus, who endured the cross. It gives the race its leader and its goal, and it complements Paul's picture of the believer's discipline.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning, God gave humanity authority over the earth, Genesis 1:28, and the first sin was a grasping at what was not given, Genesis 3:6. The pattern of the fall is a right seized for self. The pattern of redemption is the opposite, a right laid down for others, and chapter 9 is a lived example of that reversal. The apostle who refuses to take what is his by right is walking in the reverse direction from Adam.

The chapter also sits in the long story of Israel's priesthood. The tribe of Levi lived from the altar because it had no inheritance of its own, Numbers 18:20, and the whole nation was meant to be a kingdom of priests, Exodus 19:6. Paul takes up that background and says that the gospel now has its own servants, supported on the same principle, and that their work is not a trade but a stewardship.

The chapter points forward in the way it speaks of winning. The reach of the gospel to Jew and Gentile, to those under the law and those without it, is the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham that all nations will be blessed, Genesis 12:3. Paul spends himself to see that promise worked out, adapting to each group so that some may be saved. The mission to the nations is the middle of the story, between the cross and the new creation.

It also looks to the end. The prize is imperishable, and the race is not run in vain, 1 Corinthians 15:58. The story's end is a company of people from every nation before the throne, Revelation 7:9, and a Lord who rewards what was done for Him. The freedom Paul spent on others will be repaid in a world where nothing is lost, and where those who gave up their rights for others find that nothing given for the sake of Christ was wasted.

quiz.q: Why did Paul refuse to use his right to financial support at Corinth?

options.text: So that nothing would hinder the gospel of Christ.
options.note: Verse 12: he put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel.

options.text: So no one could accuse him of preaching for personal gain.
options.note: True and related, though Paul's stated reason is the broader one, not to hinder the gospel.

options.text: Because ministers should never be paid.
options.note: Paul affirms the right; the Lord prescribed that preachers live from the gospel.

options.text: Because he was not really an apostle.
options.note: He opens the chapter proving he is a genuine, free apostle.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by becoming all things to all people?

options.text: Flexing on custom to remove barriers, so that by all means he might save some.
options.note: He adapts culturally while remaining under the law of Christ, to win as many as possible.

options.text: Adapting his approach to different people to build a connection.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but it leaves out his aim, that some might be saved.

options.text: Adjusting the gospel message to please each audience.
options.note: He never edits the message; he adapts in non-essentials only.

options.text: Living however he pleased with no principles.
options.note: Verse 21: he is not outside God's law but under the law of Christ.

quiz.q: How does Paul establish that gospel workers deserve support?

options.text: From the soldier, farmer, and shepherd, the Law of Moses, and the temple, capped by the Lord's own command.
options.note: He piles up witnesses from life, Scripture, and Jesus Himself.

options.text: From his own authority as an apostle alone.
options.note: His apostleship matters, but he grounds the right much more widely.

options.text: From Greek customs about paying teachers.
options.note: He argues from Scripture and the Lord, not pagan custom.

options.text: He does not; he says workers deserve nothing.
options.note: He strongly affirms the right, then chooses not to use it.

quiz.q: What is the imperishable crown Paul runs for?

options.text: The unfading reward Christ gives to those who finish the race of faith.
options.note: Unlike the athlete's withering wreath, this crown never fades.

options.text: The believer's final salvation and glory with Christ.
options.note: Closely related and true, though Paul frames it as the imperishable prize won by running faithfully.

options.text: A literal wreath of leaves from the games.
options.note: That is the perishable crown he contrasts with the imperishable one.

options.text: Financial reward for his ministry.
options.note: He refused payment; the crown is the eternal prize.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by disciplining his body lest he be disqualified?

options.text: He calls for disciplined, persevering faith, as the mark of one who truly runs to win.
options.note: Like an athlete keeping the rules, he presses on with self-control to the end.

options.text: A sober warning that even gifted preachers must live holy, self-controlled lives.
options.note: A true implication, held within his call to disciplined perseverance to the end.

options.text: That a believer can casually lose salvation by one mistake.
options.note: It is a call to vigilance and endurance, not a theology of easily lost salvation.

options.text: That the body is evil and must be punished.
options.note: He teaches discipline for the race, not contempt for the body.

questions: Paul held real rights yet laid them down for the gospel. What legitimate right or freedom of yours might love ask you to set aside for someone else's good?
He became all things to all people to win them. Where could you flex on preferences and customs, without compromising the gospel, to reach people who are not like you?
Paul felt a holy compulsion, woe to me if I do not preach. What has God entrusted to you that you are tempted to treat as optional rather than as a calling?
The athlete trains with strict discipline for a fading wreath. What would disciplined, purposeful running look like in your walk with Christ this week?
Paul feared preaching to others yet being disqualified himself. How do you guard your own heart and life so that your faith is more than words?

translationNotes.note: Cephas is the Aramaic name for Peter; Paul names him alongside the other apostles and the Lord's brothers to show that travelling with a believing wife was an accepted apostolic practice.
Do not muzzle an ox is quoted from Deuteronomy 25:4; Paul reads it not as mere animal welfare but as a principle written for the sake of human workers, that the labourer should share in the harvest.
Disqualified translates adokimos, an athletic term for being ruled out of the prize; the verse warns of the need for disciplined perseverance, not that a genuine believer is easily cast away.
